title: Secret Interview Tests Make Big Inferences From Small Acts
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines the quirky 'secret tests' some leaders use to screen job candidates, such as watching whether they clear their coffee cup, salt their food before tasting it, or sit at the head of the table. It argues these single-signal tests are a shortcut that overreaches, turning a small observed behavior into a sweeping judgment about character or fit. The piece distinguishes between reasonable, broad-based inference gathering — watching candidates in informal settings, checking social media, asking unscripted questions — and the far riskier practice of disqualifying someone based on one idiosyncratic tell. It ultimately frames leaders who rely on a single litmus-test behavior as revealing more about their own poor judgment than about the candidate's true character.
points: Leaders often invent idiosyncratic 'secret tests' — coffee cups, salting food, messy cars — to judge candidates.
Making inferences from small acts is normal, but eliminating candidates over one act is an overreach.
Sounder secret tests include observing candidates informally, reviewing social media, and posing unscripted questions.
The best approach folds every data point into a holistic judgment rather than treating any single tell as decisive.
Leaders who lean on one quirky signal for hire/no-hire decisions are exhibiting poor decision-making, not insight.
quotes: To cut through the red tape of interview noise, some leaders rely upon secret tests to evaluate whether people possess the values and character they seek in an ideal candidate.
Making inferences from small acts is something all good decision-makers do. But eliminating a candidate based upon a simple act, gesture, or choice borders on the ridiculous.
Leaders who cling to farcical secret tests to determine who should be eliminated from consideration lack the objectivity needed to accurately assess candidates.
They may think they have landed on a secret portal into the mind of a candidate, but all they have really done is show they are comically bad at making talent decisions.
If leaders are going to put people to the test, as they should, they need to use many reasonable examples that reveal the complete portrait of a candidate.
